checks.prompt: A team is building an English text-to-speech front end and asks whether they need a sound-unit layer at all, since 'the model can read letters'. Which argument correctly settles when they do and when they do not?
checks.explanation: The layer earns its place exactly where writing and pronunciation come apart — and English is the strong case for it, since the same spelling can have different pronunciations and the same sound can be spelled many ways. Feeding sound units removes that ambiguity before the acoustic model. It can genuinely be skipped when a character-trained end-to-end model has enough data to learn the mapping itself; what you give up is control and the ability to inspect or correct a specific pronunciation, which is why front ends persist in production systems.
options: They need it whenever spelling and sound diverge and the divergence matters — English spelling is famously irregular, so words spelled identically can be said differently and words spelled differently can rhyme; converting to sound units removes that ambiguity before the acoustic model sees anything. They can skip it when an end-to-end model trained on characters learns the mapping implicitly and they do not need to inspect or correct pronunciation — the trade being less control and harder debugging
They never need it: sound units are a legacy of statistical recognition systems and modern synthesis is always trained on characters
They always need it: no neural synthesis model can be trained on characters, because the acoustic model requires a discrete finite inventory
They need it only for languages other than English, since English spelling is regular enough for a character model

checks.prompt: Describe speech as a two-layer alphabet, naming the three levels from writing down to articulation and what converts between them. Define a phoneme precisely and distinguish it from a realised sound and from variants that do not change meaning. Then explain what the third level buys you that the second alone does not, with a concrete example.
checks.expected: A correct answer must lay out three levels. The written level is letters. Below it are the sound units, reached by grapheme-to-phoneme conversion — typically a lexicon lookup with a learned model as fallback. Below those are articulatory features describing how the mouth produces each sound: for consonants whether the vocal folds vibrate, where the constriction is made, and how the airflow is shaped; for vowels the tongue's height and backness and lip rounding. A phoneme must be defined as the smallest unit that distinguishes one word from another in a language — swap it and you get a different word — which makes it an abstract contrastive category rather than an acoustic event. That must be contrasted with an actual realised sound, and with variants that count as the same category to speakers of the language even though they are physically different, such as the differently produced initial sound in two words where nobody hears them as different words. The key point about the third level must be made concretely: features turn 'these two sounds are nearly the same' from an intuition into a computable quantity, because two sounds can be compared by counting how many features they differ in — a pair differing only in whether the vocal folds vibrate is close, while a pair differing in both the place and the manner of articulation is far. That is what makes a feature-weighted distance more faithful than treating the units as opaque symbols. Noting that the inventory is discrete and finite, around forty-odd for English, and sits between text and raw audio, is a plus.

checks.prompt: A pronunciation pipeline is being assembled from parts: an English lexicon in a compact ASCII notation, a multilingual converter that emits the universal alphabet, and a library that turns those universal symbols into feature vectors. What is the risk in wiring them together, and what does each notation actually give you?
checks.explanation: The practical hazard when assembling a pipeline from separate tools is that they do not share a sound inventory: the compact ASCII notation is English-only with a fixed symbol set, the universal alphabet is open-ended and language-neutral, and other tools carry their own schemes — so a mapping table between them is required rather than optional. Their roles are also different in kind: one is a lexicon format that additionally marks stress on vowels, one is the multilingual notation to phonemise into, and the feature library is analysis, consuming universal symbols and producing articulatory vectors rather than converting text.
options: The risk is a mismatch of inventories: the compact ASCII notation is English-only with a fixed set of symbols, the universal alphabet is open-ended, and a third tool may use its own scheme — mixing them without an explicit mapping table produces nonsense. What each gives you is: the ASCII notation is a convenient English lexicon format that also encodes stress as a digit on vowels; the universal alphabet is language-neutral and the right choice for multilingual work; and the feature library is analysis rather than conversion, taking universal symbols in and producing articulatory vectors
There is no risk, because all three schemes are notational variants of one inventory and convert between each other automatically; the only difference is whether the symbols are ASCII
The risk is that the feature library also performs grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, duplicating the lexicon; the notations themselves are interchangeable
The risk is purely performance, since the universal alphabet is Unicode; the compact ASCII notation covers every language and should be used throughout

checks.prompt: Implement the analysis layer. A feature table maps a bare phoneme symbol to a tuple whose first element is a kind tag and whose remaining three elements are its articulatory features. Write `strip_stress(phoneme)` returning the pair (symbol with any trailing `0`, `1` or `2` removed, that digit as an integer or None). Write `stress_of(phoneme)` returning just that digit. Write `features(phoneme, table)` returning the three articulatory features, raising `ValueError` when the stripped symbol is not in the table. Write `feature_distance(a, b, table)` returning 0.0 when the two stripped symbols are equal and otherwise the proportion of the three features that differ. Write `phonetic_distance(source, target, table)`, a Levenshtein distance over phoneme sequences where an insertion or a deletion costs 1.0 and a substitution costs `feature_distance`. Write `is_minimal_pair(source, target, table)` returning True only when the sequences are the same length, differ in exactly one position by stripped symbol, and both symbols at that position are in the table. Write `lookup(word, lexicon, fallback=None)` where the lexicon maps a lower-case word to a list of pronunciations: return COPIES of every pronunciation it holds, lower-casing the query; when the word is absent, return a single-element list holding the result of calling `fallback(word)` if one was given, and otherwise raise `KeyError`. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The comparison in the middle is the whole argument for this representation. Two words that each differ from the reference by exactly one sound would both score exactly 1 under a plain string edit distance — the substitution is one symbol either way. Weighting by articulatory features ranks them properly: a change in voicing alone is a third of a unit, while a change in both place and manner is two thirds, which matches what a listener hears. Note also that insertions and deletions still cost a full unit, so a missing sound remains a bigger error than a slightly wrong one, which is the behaviour you want in pronunciation scoring. The stress assertions carry a separate lesson: the digit on a vowel is prosody, not identity, so it must be stripped when asking whether two sounds are the same phoneme and kept when rhythm matters. And the lookup block shows the two things a dictionary cannot do for you — a word with more than one valid pronunciation comes back with all of them and something else has to choose, and a word the dictionary has never seen needs a fallback or it fails outright.
checks.test:
TABLE = {
    "P": ("C", "voiceless", "bilabial", "stop"),
    "B": ("C", "voiced", "bilabial", "stop"),
    "T": ("C", "voiceless", "alveolar", "stop"),
    "D": ("C", "voiced", "alveolar", "stop"),
    "K": ("C", "voiceless", "velar", "stop"),
    "G": ("C", "voiced", "velar", "stop"),
    "S": ("C", "voiceless", "alveolar", "fricative"),
    "Z": ("C", "voiced", "alveolar", "fricative"),
    "M": ("C", "voiced", "bilabial", "nasal"),
    "N": ("C", "voiced", "alveolar", "nasal"),
    "AE": ("V", "voiced", "front-low", "vowel"),
    "IH": ("V", "voiced", "front-high", "vowel"),
    "AH": ("V", "voiced", "central-mid", "vowel"),
}

# Stress rides on the vowel as a trailing digit, and it is separable from identity.
assert strip_stress("AE1") == ("AE", 1)
assert strip_stress("AH0") == ("AH", 0)
assert strip_stress("IH2") == ("IH", 2)
assert strip_stress("T") == ("T", None)
assert stress_of("AE1") == 1 and stress_of("K") is None

# The feature table turns "these two sounds are nearly the same" into a number.
# Voicing alone:
assert abs(feature_distance("P", "B", TABLE) - 1 / 3) < 1e-12
assert abs(feature_distance("K", "G", TABLE) - 1 / 3) < 1e-12
assert abs(feature_distance("S", "Z", TABLE) - 1 / 3) < 1e-12
# Place alone:
assert abs(feature_distance("P", "T", TABLE) - 1 / 3) < 1e-12
# Place and manner together, which is a genuinely bigger change:
assert abs(feature_distance("P", "S", TABLE) - 2 / 3) < 1e-12
assert abs(feature_distance("B", "N", TABLE) - 2 / 3) < 1e-12
assert feature_distance("P", "P", TABLE) == 0.0
assert feature_distance("AE", "IH", TABLE) == 1 / 3

# Identity is about the phoneme, not the stress mark on it.
assert feature_distance("AE1", "AE0", TABLE) == 0.0
assert stress_of("AE1") != stress_of("AE0")
assert abs(feature_distance("AE1", "IH0", TABLE) - 1 / 3) < 1e-12

for bad in ("Q", "TH", "AE3"):
    try:
        feature_distance(bad, "P", TABLE)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad!r} must be refused")

# THE point of weighting: two one-phoneme changes that a plain string edit distance
# would both score as exactly 1 are ranked correctly against each other.
pat = ["P", "AE1", "T"]
bat = ["B", "AE1", "T"]
sat = ["S", "AE1", "T"]
pit = ["P", "IH1", "T"]
near = phonetic_distance(pat, bat, TABLE)
far = phonetic_distance(pat, sat, TABLE)
assert abs(near - 1 / 3) < 1e-12, near
assert abs(far - 2 / 3) < 1e-12, far
assert near < far, (near, far)
assert near < 1.0 and far < 1.0, "an unweighted distance would score both as 1"
assert abs(phonetic_distance(pat, pit, TABLE) - 1 / 3) < 1e-12

# Insertions and deletions still cost a whole unit, so a missing sound is a bigger
# error than a slightly wrong one.
assert phonetic_distance(pat, ["P", "AE1"], TABLE) == 1.0
assert phonetic_distance(pat, pat + ["S"], TABLE) == 1.0
assert phonetic_distance(pat, pat, TABLE) == 0.0
assert phonetic_distance([], pat, TABLE) == 3.0
assert phonetic_distance(pat, [], TABLE) == 3.0
assert phonetic_distance(["P"], ["S"], TABLE) < phonetic_distance(["P"], [], TABLE)

# A minimal pair is the evidence that two sounds contrast: same length, exactly one
# position different.
assert is_minimal_pair(pat, bat, TABLE) is True
assert is_minimal_pair(pat, pit, TABLE) is True
assert is_minimal_pair(pat, pat, TABLE) is False
assert is_minimal_pair(pat, ["B", "IH1", "T"], TABLE) is False
assert is_minimal_pair(pat, ["P", "AE1"], TABLE) is False
# ...and stress is not a phoneme difference, so it does not make a minimal pair.
assert is_minimal_pair(["P", "AE1", "T"], ["P", "AE0", "T"], TABLE) is False

# A lexicon returns EVERY pronunciation it knows, which is why a lookup alone
# cannot resolve a word whose spelling maps to more than one sound.
LEXICON = {
    "cat": [["K", "AE1", "T"]],
    "read": [["R", "IY1", "D"], ["R", "EH1", "D"]],
}
assert lookup("cat", LEXICON) == [["K", "AE1", "T"]]
assert lookup("CAT", LEXICON) == [["K", "AE1", "T"]]
assert len(lookup("read", LEXICON)) == 2, lookup("read", LEXICON)
# The returned lists are copies, so a caller cannot corrupt the lexicon.
got = lookup("cat", LEXICON)
got[0][0] = "G"
assert LEXICON["cat"] == [["K", "AE1", "T"]]

# A word the lexicon has never seen is the common case for names and new coinages,
# so a fallback is not optional -- without one the failure is explicit.
assert lookup("zorblax", LEXICON, fallback=lambda w: ["Z", "AO1", "R", "B"]) == \
    [["Z", "AO1", "R", "B"]]
try:
    lookup("zorblax", LEXICON)
except KeyError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown word with no fallback must be refused")

checks.prompt: A synthesis front end mispronounces three things: a sentence containing the word 'read' in the past tense, a customer's unusual surname, and a line reading '$5 in the 1990s'. Which diagnosis and set of fixes is correct?
checks.explanation: Three genuinely different problems that get blamed on one component. A word whose spelling has more than one pronunciation is ambiguous in principle: the dictionary honestly returns both, and choosing needs grammatical context. An unfamiliar name is out of vocabulary, which is what a learned fallback exists for — without one such words fail silently. And numbers, currency and abbreviations must be expanded into words before any sound conversion happens at all; that normalisation step is where the majority of front-end mistakes actually occur.
options: Three different failures. A word whose spelling maps to more than one pronunciation cannot be resolved by a lexicon lookup at all — it needs part-of-speech tagging or a context-aware model to choose. An unusual surname is simply not in the dictionary, so a learned fallback is required or such words are silently dropped or mangled. And the currency and decade are a TEXT NORMALISATION failure that happens BEFORE any sound conversion: numbers, abbreviations and symbols must be expanded to words first, which is where most front-end errors actually live
All three are dictionary coverage problems, solved by adding the missing entries to the lexicon, including one entry per numeric form
The past-tense word and the surname are both handled by stripping stress digits before lookup; the currency problem is a limitation of the sound inventory, which has no symbol for a currency sign
All three indicate the wrong phoneme inventory was selected; switching to the universal alphabet resolves the ambiguity, the missing name and the number expansion together

checks.prompt: Four tools are on the table: an English pronunciation dictionary, a learned English converter, a multilingual phonemiser producing the universal alphabet, and a feature-vector library. Say what each is for and its limitation. Then advise on three tasks: an English synthesis front end, a research project measuring how similar two languages' sound inventories are, and fuzzy matching of customer names in a database. Give a recommendation and reasoning for each.
checks.expected: A correct answer must characterise all four. The dictionary is fast and exact for English words it contains, and its limitations are no coverage of unknown words, English only, and no way to choose between multiple pronunciations of one spelling. The learned converter handles unknown words, names and coinages end to end for English, at the cost of being heavier and occasionally wrong. The multilingual phonemiser produces the language-neutral alphabet across many languages and is the standard front-end tool, at the cost of an external binary dependency and variable quality per language. The feature-vector library converts universal symbols into articulatory vectors and computes distance — it is analysis rather than conversion, so it does not turn text into sounds at all. The recommendations must follow. An English synthesis front end should combine the dictionary with a learned fallback for out-of-vocabulary words, so common words are exact and names still work — with text normalisation ahead of both. Comparing two languages' inventories is a phonetic-distance question over the universal alphabet, so the phonemiser feeds the feature library; a dictionary in an English-only ASCII notation cannot express non-English sounds. Fuzzy name matching in a database does not need real pronunciations at all: a cheap phonetic hashing scheme is coarse and lossy but exactly right for that job, and reaching for a full front end there is unnecessary cost. A strong answer names the general rule — go fully end-to-end on characters only when you have the data and do not need to inspect or correct specific pronunciations — and notes that mixing tools requires a mapping between their sound inventories.
